name: PRP facial (vampire facial)

lead: A PRP facial, popularly the vampire facial, uses plasma concentrated from your own blood, applied during microneedling, to rejuvenate skin: smoother texture, softer fine lines and improved acne scars.

PRP is blood plasma with red cells removed and platelets raised to about three to five times normal levels. Proponents say its growth factors signal skin cells to repair tissue and build collagen, while microneedling creates controlled micro-injuries that start healing. Reviews describe PRP evidence as mixed across conditions, and small studies exist for skin rejuvenation.

paras: A clinician draws a small blood sample, spins it in a centrifuge and applies the plasma to the face, most often with microneedling. Some do-it-yourself communities also describe home versions. Redness and swelling settle within days, and people usually repeat sessions.

Redness, swelling, bruising and numbness are usually brief. The main documented harm is infection from unlicensed providers using inadequately sterilised equipment: in 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to an Albuquerque spa, after a 2018 state warning. The FDA does not regulate PRP itself, though the preparation devices need clearance.

chain: Better texture, fewer fine lines and scars
angle.text: Users have PRP facials, popularly the vampire facial, for rejuvenated skin, smoother texture, fewer fine lines and softer acne scars. Your own platelets applied with microneedling are said to trigger skin repair and a collagen response. Small studies exist for skin rejuvenation.

lead: A PRP facial, popularly known as a vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure in which blood drawn from the patient is centrifuged to produce platelet-rich plasma (PRP), which is then applied to the face, most often together with microneedling. It is marketed for skin rejuvenation, fine lines, texture and acne scars, with the aim of a smoother, brighter-looking complexion [1][2].

PRP is a concentrate of plasma from a person's own blood with red blood cells removed and platelets kept, usually raised to about three to five times normal levels [1]. Proponents say the platelets' growth factors, delivered into the tiny channels microneedling makes in the skin, speed the healing response and the building of collagen, so that skin looks fresher and scars look shallower [3][1].

Its evidence base is described as mixed: PRP appears to help in some conditions and not in others, and facial rejuvenation is one of several aesthetic uses described as having limited support [1]. The procedure became widely known after a March 2013 social-media post by the celebrity Kim Kardashian West, which a Google Trends analysis links to a surge in searches for 'vampire facial' [4][2].

The main documented harm is infection transmission when procedures are performed by unlicensed operators. New Mexico health officials warned in 2018 about a business offering vampire facials, and in 2024 the CDC reported that three women had been diagnosed with HIV after treatments at an Albuquerque spa [1][2]. The treatment has also been discussed in looksmaxxing forums, including by members who describe doing PRP microneedling themselves [5][6].

PRP not regulated by FDA; preparation devices require clearance [1]

paras: Blood is drawn, spun in a centrifuge and separated so that a plasma fraction rich in platelets remains. It may be activated before use, though activation is not required.[1] The product is applied to the skin during or after microneedling, or injected. The practice sits within the older category of autologous blood therapy, which dermatologists used widely in the early twentieth century before abandoning it for lack of evidence; interest returned in the 2000s.[2]

sections.h: How the procedure is done in clinics
paras: In a clinic setting, blood is drawn, spun in a centrifuge and separated so that a platelet-rich fraction remains; the plasma may be activated with thrombin or calcium chloride, though activation is optional [1]. Wikipedia classes PRP by its white blood cell and fibrin content into leukocyte-rich, leukocyte-reduced and platelet-rich fibrin forms, and notes that the final product varies between patients and facilities [1].

The plasma is spread over the face during or after microneedling, which repeatedly punctures the skin with tiny sterile needles in a procedure also called collagen induction therapy or dermarolling [7]. For hair loss, Wikipedia describes a typical PRP course as at least three monthly treatments followed by maintenance, and aesthetic skin protocols are likewise commonly described as repeated sessions [1].

The term platelet-rich plasma was first used in 1954, platelet banks followed in the 1960s, and it entered surgical use in the late 1980s and hair-loss research in 2006.[1] Vampire facials became popular in the 2010s after celebrity endorsements.[1] A 2024 study used Google Trends data to examine how social media affected the popularity of the vampire facial.[8]

Wikipedia states that the term platelet-rich plasma dates to 1954, that PRP was used in hematology in the 1970s and in surgery in the late 1980s, and that interest in hair-loss treatment began around 2006 [1]. The cosmetic version sits within the older category of autologous blood therapy, which dermatologists used in the early twentieth century and left for lack of supporting evidence, with interest returning in the 2000s [2].

The 'vampire facial' name entered mainstream use in March 2013, when Kim Kardashian West posted a selfie of the treatment with the hashtag vampire facial [4][2]. A letter analysing Google Trends data from 2010 to 2020 reported a massive rise in worldwide web searches that month, with average monthly interest rising from between 0 and 1 before 2013 to 11.4 from 2013 to 2020, and found 'vampire facial' searches higher in the UK, Ireland and Australia than in the US [4]. The authors argue that celebrity-sensationalised procedures raise consumer demand, while noting that the data show timing rather than proof of cause [4]. Wikipedia adds that she later said she regretted it [2].

PRP contains growth factors and cytokines. Proponents say microneedling and PRP together stimulate collagen production, and clinicians have published technique descriptions such as a single-handed method for combining the two.[3]

Practitioners and forum members distinguish several related preparations. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) is a fibrin-matrix form that Wikipedia says is used as an autologous 'vampire filler' by licensed surgeons and is generally not described as autohemotherapy [2]. Some forum users call PRF preparations 'biofillers' and discuss them for under-eye hollows and the jawline [5]. PRP can also be injected rather than applied through microneedling channels, and the same concentrate is used on the scalp for hair loss [1].

Wikipedia's overview of PRP describes the evidence across conditions as mixed, with tentative support for knee osteoarthritis, reported benefit for alopecia areata and androgenetic alopecia, and a 2024 meta-analysis reporting faster healing of venous and diabetic foot ulcers; it describes the evidence for aesthetic use as thin [1]. It also says adverse effects in trials are generally low [1].

Microneedling's own research includes a 2012 trial on upper lip wrinkles and a 2016 split-face study of PRP with microneedling for atrophic acne scars, according to Wikipedia, which says the efficacy of microneedling combined with PRP remains uncertain pending further studies [7]. Skin-specific literature on the vampire facial itself includes a 2021 technique paper on combining microneedling with PRP and a 2024 analysis of its online popularity, neither of which reports efficacy outcomes [3][8].

Reported effects include redness, swelling, bruising and numbness, usually resolving within about two days, though some people have taken a week or more.[2] The central safety concern is providers without infection-control training. In 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that at least one business offering vampire facials could potentially spread HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and in 2024 the CDC announced that three women treated at an Albuquerque spa had been diagnosed with HIV. Officials found the operator was unlicensed and had reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment without sterilisation; about 200 other former clients tested negative.[1][2]

In 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that at least one business offering vampire facials could potentially spread HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C [2]. In April 2024 the CDC announced that three women treated at an Albuquerque spa had been diagnosed with HIV; the operator was found to be unlicensed and to have reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment without sterilisation, and about 200 other former clients tested negative [1][2][7]. Wikipedia's microneedling article notes that no testing for other blood-borne infections was mentioned in the report it cites [7].
The cluster is described in the sources as a failure of licensing and infection control rather than a property of PRP itself; the warnings stress providers with infection-control training [2][7].

In the United States the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, so its clinical use is considered off-label, while the devices used to prepare it require FDA clearance.[1] Intramuscular PRP injections were removed from the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list in 2011.[1]

Published literature specific to the vampire facial consists of a 2021 technique paper on combining microneedling with PRP[3] and a 2024 analysis of its online popularity,[8] neither of which reports efficacy outcomes. Wikipedia's overview of PRP describes evidence across conditions as mixed and reports positive studies for hair loss and for some wounds, while stating that claims for some aesthetic uses lack supporting evidence.[1] Large randomised trials establishing the size or durability of facial benefit have not been reported.

A looksmax.org member has posted about ordering equipment for a home setup to perform PRP vampire facials and related PRF 'biofiller' preparations.[5] Replies in the thread are largely jokes. Clinicians and health agencies, in contrast, emphasise licensed settings because of infection risk.[1][2]

Looksmax.org threads describe members using PRP microneedling for acne scars and reporting that skin looked better on camera the day after and that people noticed [6]. Another member describes ordering equipment to set up PRP and PRF preparation, citing a wish for sterile tools and a lower cost than clinics, and plans monthly vampire facials alongside periodic biofiller injections [5]. Replies in these threads mix interest with jokes. Health agencies in the sources emphasise licensed settings because of the infection risk [2][7].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the vampire facial appears in posts by members reporting scar treatment and by members planning to prepare PRP and PRF 'biofillers' for personal use [5][6].

claims.claim: PRP microneedling can improve skin quality and slow visible ageing.
Doing PRP at home or in a self-run setup is a workable alternative to a clinic.
PRF 'biofillers' can replace hyaluronic acid filler.
It is safe because it uses your own blood.
